stem: Stage 1 of a pattern is an equilateral triangle with sides of 9 cm. Each later stage is made from the one before: every side is divided into three equal parts, and the middle part is replaced by the two other sides of a small equilateral triangle that points outwards. The process continues without end.

stem: Stage 2 has 12 sides, each of length 3 cm. The area of a stage means the area enclosed by its outline.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that stage \(n\) has \(3 \times 4^{\,n-1}\) sides, each of length \(9\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{n-1}\) cm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence show that the perimeter of stage \(n\) is \(27\left(\frac{4}{3}\right)^{n-1}\) cm, and explain why the perimeter does not approach a limit as \(n\) increases.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the smallest value of \(n\) for which the perimeter of stage \(n\) is greater than 100 cm.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The area of an equilateral triangle with side \(s\) is \(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}s^2\). Show that the total area of the new small triangles added in going from stage \(n\) to stage \(n + 1\) is \(\dfrac{27\sqrt{3}}{4}\left(\dfrac{4}{9}\right)^{n-1}\) cm\(^2\).

parts.label: e
parts.text: Find the limit of the area of stage \(n\) as \(n\) increases, giving your answer in the form \(k\sqrt{3}\), where \(k \in \mathbb{Q}\).

idea: Track three geometric sequences: the number of sides (×4 each stage), the length of a side (×\(\frac{1}{3}\)) and the area added (one new triangle on every side, each with \(\frac{1}{9}\) of the area of the last ones, so ×\(\frac{4}{9}\)). A geometric series has a sum to infinity only when \(|r| < 1\).

solution.label: a
steps: Each side is replaced by 4 sides (two thirds of the old side stay, and two new sides are added), so the number of sides is multiplied by 4 at each stage: \(3, 12, 48, \ldots = 3 \times 4^{\,n-1}\).
Each new side is one third of an old side, so side lengths are \(9, 3, 1, \ldots = 9\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{n-1}\).

solution.label: b
steps: This is a geometric sequence with common ratio \(\frac{4}{3} > 1\), so the perimeter grows without bound.
solution.answer: \(P_n = 27\left(\frac{4}{3}\right)^{n-1}\); no limit, since the ratio \(\frac{4}{3}\) is greater than 1

solution.label: d
steps: Going from stage \(n\) to stage \(n + 1\), one new triangle is added on each of the \(3 \times 4^{\,n-1}\) sides. Its side is one third of a side of stage \(n\): \(\dfrac{9}{3}\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{n-1} = 3\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{n-1}\).
Check with \(n = 1\): three triangles of side 3 have total area \(3 \times \dfrac{9\sqrt{3}}{4} = \dfrac{27\sqrt{3}}{4}\).

solution.label: e
steps: The added areas form a geometric series with first term \(\dfrac{27\sqrt{3}}{4}\) and ratio \(\dfrac{4}{9}\). Since \(\left|\frac{4}{9}\right| < 1\), it has a sum to infinity:
So the area stays finite (\(\frac{8}{5}\) of the original triangle) even though the perimeter grows without bound.

stem: Priya buys a motorbike for $12 000. Its value decreases by 15% each year.
On the same day her brother Arjun invests $5000 in an account paying a nominal annual interest rate of 6%, compounded monthly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the value of the motorbike after 3 years.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the percentage of its original value that the motorbike has lost after 3 years.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the number of complete years after which the value of the motorbike first falls below half of its original value.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the amount in Arjun’s account after 3 years.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Find the number of complete years after which the amount in Arjun’s account first exceeds the value of the motorbike.

parts.label: f
parts.text: Arjun wants his $5000 to grow to $8000 in 5 years. Find the nominal annual interest rate, compounded monthly, that he would need.

idea: Depreciation of 15% multiplies the value by 0.85 each year. Monthly compounding at a nominal 6% multiplies the amount by \(1 + \frac{0.06}{12}\) each month, so \(12n\) times in \(n\) years. To compare the two, list the values year by year.

solution.label: c
steps: Half of the original value is $6000. Solve \(12\,000 \times 0.85^n < 6000\), that is \(0.85^n < 0.5\).

solution.label: e
steps: Compare the two at the end of each year:
Year 3: \(A = 5983.40\), \(V = 7369.50\). The motorbike is worth more.
The account grows each year and the motorbike loses value each year, so once the account is ahead it stays ahead.

solution.label: f
steps: Let the nominal rate be \(r\%\). Then \(5000\left(1 + \dfrac{r}{1200}\right)^{60} = 8000\), so \(\left(1 + \dfrac{r}{1200}\right)^{60} = 1.6\).
\(r = 1200 \times 0.0078641\ldots = 9.4369\ldots\) (a finance solver gives the same value).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the first four terms of the expansion in ascending powers of \(x\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the coefficient of \(x^2\) in the expansion of \((1 + 2x)^6(3 - x)\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your answer to part (a), with a suitable value of \(x\), to find an estimate of \(1.02^6\). Give your answer to five decimal places.

parts.label: d
parts.text: In the expansion of \((1 + 2x)^6(1 + ax)^2\), where \(a\) is a constant, the coefficient of \(x\) is zero. Find the value of \(a\), and hence find the coefficient of \(x^2\).

idea: The general term of \((1 + 2x)^6\) is \(\binom{6}{r}(2x)^r\). In a product of two brackets, a term in \(x^2\) comes from every pair of terms whose powers of \(x\) add to 2: list those pairs and add their products.

solution.label: c
steps: The terms left out are very small (the next one is \(240 \times 0.01^4 = 0.0000024\)), so five decimal places are reliable.

stem: Two cyclists start a training plan on the same day.
Ana cycles 10 km on day 1 and increases her distance by 1.25 km each day.
Ben cycles 10 km on day 1 and increases his distance by 7% each day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the distance Ana cycles on day 10.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the total distance Ana cycles in the first 10 days.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the distance Ben cycles on day 10.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the total distance Ben cycles in the first 10 days.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Find the first day on which Ben cycles further than Ana.

parts.label: f
parts.text: Find the number of days after which Ben’s total distance first exceeds Ana’s total distance.

idea: Ana’s daily distances form an arithmetic sequence and Ben’s a geometric sequence. A geometric sequence with \(r > 1\) eventually overtakes any arithmetic one, but the totals catch up later than the daily distances, because Ben has to make up the distance he lost on the earlier days.

solution.label: e
steps: We need the smallest \(n\) with \(10 \times 1.07^{\,n-1} > 10 + 1.25(n - 1)\). Use a table or the graphs of both sides on a GDC.
Day 17: Ben \(10 \times 1.07^{16} = 29.52\ldots\), Ana \(30\). Ana is still further.
Day 18: Ben \(10 \times 1.07^{17} = 31.58\ldots\), Ana \(31.25\). Ben is further.

solution.label: f
steps: After 24 days: Ben \(581.7\ldots\) km, Ana \(585\) km.
After 25 days: Ben \(632.4\ldots\) km, Ana \(625\) km.

So Ben’s total first exceeds Ana’s after 25 days, seven days after he first cycles further on a single day. Ben needs those seven days to make up the distance he lost while Ana was cycling further each day.

stem: The loudness of a sound, \(L\) decibels (dB), is given by \(L = 10\log_{10}\left(\dfrac{I}{I_0}\right)\), where \(I\) is the intensity of the sound and \(I_0\) is a fixed reference intensity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find \(L\) for a sound of intensity \(10^5 I_0\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that if the intensity of a sound is multiplied by \(k\), its loudness increases by \(10\log_{10} k\) dB.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A lawnmower is 20 dB louder than a conversation. Find how many times greater the intensity of the lawnmower is.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the intensity of a sound of loudness 35 dB, giving your answer in the form \(p\sqrt{10}\,I_0\), where \(p \in \mathbb{Z}\).

parts.label: e
parts.text: One machine produces a sound of loudness 60 dB. Two identical machines together produce twice the intensity. Given that \(\log_{10} 2 \approx 0.301\), find the loudness of the two machines together.

parts.label: f
parts.text: A factory has \(n\) identical machines, each producing 60 dB, so that their intensities add. Find the least value of \(n\) for which the total loudness is at least 75 dB.

idea: Use the laws of logarithms: \(\log_{10}(kx) = \log_{10} k + \log_{10} x\). Multiplying the intensity adds a fixed amount to the loudness. To go from loudness back to intensity, undo the logarithm with a power of 10.

solution.label: b
steps: So the loudness increases by \(10\log_{10} k\).

solution.label: f
steps: By part (b) with \(k = n\): we need \(60 + 10\log_{10} n \ge 75\), so \(\log_{10} n \ge 1.5\) and \(n \ge 10^{1.5} = 10\sqrt{10}\).

stem: This question is about the product of four consecutive integers, \(n(n + 1)(n + 2)(n + 3)\), where \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Expand and simplify \(\left(n^2 + 3n + 1\right)^2\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prove that \(n(n + 1)(n + 2)(n + 3) + 1 = \left(n^2 + 3n + 1\right)^2\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence, without a calculator, find the value of \(\sqrt{99 \times 100 \times 101 \times 102 + 1}\).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Prove that \(n^2 + 3n + 1\) is odd for every integer \(n\).

parts.label: e
parts.text: Lena works out \(\sqrt{n(n + 1)(n + 2)(n + 3) + 1}\) for \(n = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5\) and finds 5, 11, 19, 29 and 41. She claims that for every positive integer \(n\), this square root is a prime number. Find the smallest value of \(n\) that shows Lena’s claim is false.

idea: Pair the outer factors and the inner factors: \(n(n + 3) = n^2 + 3n\) and \((n + 1)(n + 2) = n^2 + 3n + 2\). With \(m = n^2 + 3n\), the product plus 1 is \(m(m + 2) + 1 = (m + 1)^2\). A claim about every \(n\) is disproved by one counterexample.

solution.label: b
steps: Adding 1 gives \(n^4 + 6n^3 + 11n^2 + 6n + 1\), which is \(\left(n^2 + 3n + 1\right)^2\) by part (a).

solution.label: d
steps: \(n\) and \(n + 3\) differ by 3, an odd number, so one of them is even and one is odd. Hence \(n(n + 3)\) is even.
An even number plus 1 is odd, so \(n^2 + 3n + 1\) is odd for every integer \(n\).

solution.label: e
steps: By part (b), the square root is \(n^2 + 3n + 1\) (which is positive for every positive integer \(n\)). One value of \(n\) that gives a number that is not prime is enough to disprove the claim.
Lena has checked \(n = 1\) to 5. Next, \(n = 6\): \(36 + 18 + 1 = 55 = 5 \times 11\), which is not prime.

stem: A geometric series has first term 6 and common ratio \(\dfrac{x - 2}{3}\), where \(x \in \mathbb{R}\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the set of values of \(x\) for which the series has a sum to infinity.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the sum to infinity when \(x = 3.5\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the value of \(x\) for which the sum to infinity is 9.

parts.label: d
parts.text: When \(x = 3.5\), find the least number of terms for which the sum of the series is greater than 11.99.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Find the set of all possible values of the sum to infinity.

idea: A geometric series has a sum to infinity exactly when \(-1 < r < 1\), and then \(S_\infty = \dfrac{u_1}{1 - r}\). To find the possible sums, see how \(\dfrac{6}{1 - r}\) changes as \(r\) moves across the interval \(-1 < r < 1\).

solution.label: c
steps: \(\dfrac{x - 2}{3} = \dfrac{1}{3}\) gives \(x = 3\). This lies in \(-1 < x < 5\), so the sum to infinity exists.

solution.label: d
steps: \(2^{10} = 1024\) is too small and \(2^{11} = 2048\) is large enough.

solution.label: e
steps: As \(x\) runs over \(-1 < x < 5\), \(r\) takes every value in \(-1 < r < 1\), so \(1 - r\) takes every value in \(0 < 1 - r < 2\).
\(S_\infty = \dfrac{6}{1 - r}\). As \(1 - r\) goes from just above 0 up towards 2, \(\dfrac{6}{1 - r}\) decreases from arbitrarily large values towards 3, without reaching 3.
So \(S_\infty\) can be any number greater than 3.
